title: A Homecoming for the Semester
premise: Wren Winterbourne has her senior year mapped out: win the state debate championship, escape to a college far from her parents' suffocating expectations, and never look back. But when she inherits her late grandmother's recipe box, she discovers index cards that aren't recipes at all — they're instructions, warnings, and confessions revealing that the Winterbourne women have guarded something in the town of Hollow Creek for generations, and Wren is the last heir. As she deciphers the cards with help from three unlikely friends, she learns her grandmother didn't die naturally; she was protecting Wren from a choice the family has dodged for a century. In the end, Wren must choose between sealing the family legacy away forever or claiming it on her own terms — and she finds a third path, breaking the inheritance open so it belongs to everyone who helped her carry it.
about_author: Orsen Lockridge is the pen name of a former high school debate coach who spent twelve years watching teenagers argue brilliantly about everything except their own lives. They write young adult fiction about kids who are better with words than they are with silence.

chapters.title: Ninety-Seven Days
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. She counts down to graduation while rehearsing a debate case at the kitchen table; her parents talk over her about her future as if she isn't there. Beat: restless resentment disguised as ambition.

chapters.title: The Eulogy I Didn't Write
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. At Grandma June's funeral, relatives she barely knows trade stories about a woman Wren realizes she never really asked questions of. Her mother refuses to discuss the will. Beat: grief sharpened by regret.

chapters.title: What's Left in the Box
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The lawyer hands over June's recipe box — the only thing willed directly to Wren. The first card she pulls isn't for pie; it reads 'For the girl who wins arguments: start with what you can't say.' Beat: eerie curiosity.

chapters.title: Cards That Aren't Recipes
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, late night. She sorts the box: half are genuine recipes, half are coded instructions referencing places in Hollow Creek and a word repeated across decades — 'the Keeping.' Beat: fascination tipping into unease.

chapters.title: Debate Practice, Distraction Included
chapters.summary: Dual POV with teammate Theo Okafor, who notices Wren is off her game. Their partnership is all banter and no vulnerability. She almost tells him about the cards; doesn't. Beat: loneliness inside competence.

chapters.title: The House on Larkspur Lane
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Following card one, she visits June's shuttered house and finds a locked cellar door and fresh footprints in dust that shouldn't have any. Someone else has been here. Beat: first real fear.

chapters.title: Marisol Knows Something
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The school's outcast — who once claimed her own family had 'Keeping business' before everyone laughed — catches Wren leaving the house. Instead of mocking her, Marisol says only: 'So it picked you too.' Beat: wary alliance offered.

chapters.title: Labels
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A college interview goes perfectly until her mother answers every question for her. That night Wren rereads June's card: 'They will tell you who you are. Write it yourself.' Beat: the theme crystallizes into personal stakes.

chapters.title: Three Cards Deep
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Card two leads to the library's restricted archive, where June's name appears on a ledger dated 1948 — impossible, unless names are inherited along with duties. Beat: the mystery widens beyond one woman.

chapters.title: Theo Asks the Wrong Question
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. He confronts Wren about her distraction; she deflects with a cruel joke about his scholarship anxieties. He walks. Beat: self-sabotage — Wren hurts people the way she's been hurt.

chapters.title: Marisol's Version of the Story
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Over gas-station coffee, Marisol reveals her great-aunt was a Keeper who died 'of exhaustion' after refusing to pass the duty on, and that the Keeping 'doesn't like being refused.' Beat: stakes made mortal.

chapters.title: The Cellar Opens
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Using a key hidden in a hollowed recipe card, Wren opens the cellar: shelves of boxes, one per generation, each holding a Keeper's final testimony. June's box is empty except for a mirror. Beat: awe curdling into dread — the empty box means unfinished business.

chapters.title: Interim: What the Mirror Shows
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, dreamlike interlude. In the mirror she sees not herself but a line of women, each mouthing words she can't hear. She wakes with ink on her palm. Beat: the inheritance becomes literal and bodily.

chapters.title: Rehearsal Without a Partner
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Debate regionals approach; she runs cases alone and loses to a novice in practice. Her coach warns her that winning alone isn't winning. Beat: humility beginning, resisted.

chapters.title: Apology, Poorly Delivered
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Wren attempts an apology structured like a rebuttal — claims, evidence, conclusion. Theo laughs despite himself but doesn't forgive yet. Beat: earned partial repair; found family starts awkwardly.

chapters.title: Someone Is Reading Over My Shoulder
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Her research notes go missing from her locker and reappear annotated in handwriting matching June's ledger. A stranger at the edge of campus watches her leave. Beat: hunted feeling established.

chapters.title: The Hollow Creek Historical Society
chapters.summary: Ensemble scene, Wren POV. Wren, Marisol, and eventually Theo visit the historical society, where curator Mr. Aldous Vane is charmingly helpful — and asks one question too many about the recipe box. Beat: reader suspects what Wren doesn't.

chapters.title: Card Seven: The Rule of Three
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A card warns: 'A Keeper cannot carry it alone, cannot refuse it alone, cannot give it away alone.' Wren realizes the friends she's pulling in aren't optional — they're structural. Beat: found family reframed as necessity, then chosen.

chapters.title: Mother's Memory, Unlocked
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Wren presses her mother about June; her mother finally admits she was offered the Keeping and refused, and that June's death came weeks later. Guilt, not indifference, built her control freak armor. Beat: antagonist softened into tragic mirror.

chapters.title: Regionals
chapters.summary: Theo and Wren's POV alternating through the tournament. They win on teamwork, not brilliance — and Wren realizes arguing with someone beats arguing at them. Beat: external victory mirroring internal shift.

chapters.title: Vane Makes His Offer
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Vane reveals he's from a rival lineage that wants the Keeping dissolved — sealed, hoarded, controlled. He offers Wren freedom from the burden if she surrenders the box. Beat: temptation with a plausible face.

chapters.title: What the Keeping Actually Is
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV, archive chapter. The trio deciphers the core secret: the Keeping is a repository of the town's erased histories — every person Hollow Creek decided to forget. The Keepers remember them so they aren't fully gone. Beat: theme lands — inheritance as memory, identity as witness.

chapters.title: The Empty Chair Testimony
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. In June's testimony (hidden in the recipe box's false bottom), June confesses she delayed naming a successor hoping Wren would choose it freely — and that Vane's family caused the 'exhaustion' deaths. Beat: grief recontextualized; rage kindled.

chapters.title: Falling Apart on Schedule
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Midterms, the case, the Keeping, and her mother collide; Wren burns out spectacularly, quitting debate mid-practice. Beat: darkest personal hour before the plot's darkest hour.

chapters.title: Sixty-One Days
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Bedridden with stress, Wren rereads every card and sees June's arc: a woman who also tried to do it alone. The lesson isn't 'be strong'; it's 'don't be alone.' Beat: turning point inward.

chapters.title: The Kitchen Table Truce
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Wren and her mother have their first honest argument — not won, but heard. Mother admits fear, not disappointment. No resolution, but the door opens. Beat: reconciliation begun, realistically incomplete.

chapters.title: Vane Escalates
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The historical society 'reorganizes' its archives; Marisol's family records vanish. Vane's message is clear: cooperate or be forgotten next. Beat: threat turns personal and immediate.

chapters.title: Thirty Days
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. June's final card activates: the Keeping must be formally accepted or refused by solstice — thirty days — or it collapses, erasing every memory it holds, including pieces of the Keepers themselves. Beat: ticking clock armed.

chapters.title: Recruiting the Found Family
chapters.summary: Ensemble. Wren formally asks Theo and Marisol to stand with her — not as helpers but as co-Keepers, testing whether the rule of three can be broken into something new. The Keeping responds: the cellar lights accept all three names. Beat: hope through innovation.

chapters.title: Vane's Counterargument
chapters.summary: Vane's POV chapter. His family lost everything to the town's forgetting and believes memory should be curated, not communal. He's not wrong about pain — only about the cure. Beat: antagonist humanized; thematic debate sharpened.

chapters.title: Sabotage
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Someone torches the Larkspur house's porch; the cellar survives, barely. Police call it electrical. Nobody believes that. Beat: physical danger arrives; trust tested under pressure.

chapters.title: The Argument Wren Can't Win
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Vane corners her privately with the strongest version of his case: the Keeping cost the women their lives, and Wren is repeating their mistake with better branding. She has no rebuttal. Beat: crisis of conviction.

chapters.title: Twenty-Two Days: The Refusal Draft
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. She drafts a formal refusal — the safe exit Vane offered — and can't sign it, because refusal means the forgotten stay forgotten. Beat: identity resolved through action, not declaration.

chapters.title: Solstice Eve
chapters.summary: Ensemble. The trio prepares the acceptance rite in the cellar; Vane arrives with the historical society board to legally block them. Her mother shows up uninvited — on which side, unknown. Beat: all threads converge.

chapters.title: The Rite Interrupted
chapters.summary: Climax part one, Wren's POV. Mid-rite, Vane seizes the box; the Keeping destabilizes, and memories begin bleeding out — Wren starts losing her own name. Marisol anchors her; Theo completes the circuit. Beat: terror, sacrifice, teamwork.

chapters.title: What Wren Says to Vane
chapters.summary: Climax part two. Wren doesn't out-argue Vane — she offers him what he actually needs: his family's erased history restored into the shared record, named and mourned. He stands down, undone by being seen. Beat: the debater wins by refusing to treat it as a debate.

chapters.title: Acceptance
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The rite completes: the Keeping passes to three names, and the mirror shows not a line of solitary women but a circle. Her mother witnesses it and weeps. Beat: catharsis; inheritance transformed.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Seventeen Days
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Fallout and repair: the historical society reforms under new stewardship including Marisol; Vane, diminished but not destroyed, donates his family's records. Beat: consequences honored, world changed.

chapters.title: State Finals
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren returns for the championship she once needed to escape herself — and loses in the final round, and finds she minds far less than expected. Her mother in the audience, applauding. Beat: the old goal dethroned gracefully.

chapters.title: Graduation Day: Ninety-Seven Days Later
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, closing. At graduation, Wren receives her diploma and, afterward, adds her own card to the box — addressed to whoever comes next, ending with 'You get to choose what you carry.' She leaves for college with the box packed beside her, not behind her. Beat: full-circle resolution; identity chosen, family expanded, future open.
